rv.q: Lucy Kirkwood’s clever and funny play feels just as potent – if not more so.
O’Riordan’s economical, fluid production makes the play feel alive and timely, if perhaps not quite a modern classic.
Along the way, the play unearths past romantic entanglements and jealousies that are ultimately less interesting than the central dilemma.
And if the moralising falls flat, I was content to enjoy the company of three fine actors.
The point that Kirkwood makes is urgent and unsettling.
My principal problem, then as now, is that I struggle to believe in Rose, Hazel and Robin as retired nuclear scientists.
What I expected to be a nice, sweet Friday-night post-work watch turned out to be funny, thought-provoking, unsettling and ultimately deeply moving.
The Children leaves a scorching print on its audience.
Lucy Kirkwood’s gripping, darkly funny drama is directed by Artistic Director Rachel O’Riordan, starring the Olivier Award-nominated Meera Syal.
Rachel O’Riordan fields the collision of bourgeois etiquette, petty resentments, and existential destruction more or less perfectly.
This intriguing and thoughtful production is highly relevant in the turbulent and uncertain world in which we live.
Kirkwood’s writing is still a marvel, strong on little grace notes that bring the dialogue alive.
This sumptuous design is almost too good for the play.
The play’s shortcomings are still laid bare in this new production, but it’s an exciting chance to see a modern gem, that still has pertinent things to say a decade on from its premiere.
Rachel O’Riordan directs, and has created a definitive production of this important play.

For anyone looking for a play that does not offer easy answers, or who enjoys watching three experienced actors slowly reveal the history and tension between their characters, The Children is well worth seeing.
To express such complex emotions with such naturalness is, in itself, a testament to the skill of the playwright, director and actors.
Meera Syal really gets to the heart of the play.
Under O’Riordan’s assured direction, this revival confirms the play as significant and stimulating in its exploration of the weight of responsibility in the wake of environmental disaster.
This 10-year anniversary production of The Children is a phenomenal revival that remains pertinent in a world still deeply concerned with fuelling our enormous demand for electricity.
In the end, we are offered the sketches of what could be a stirring, thought-provoking play.
It didn't wow me. It didn't make me go: 'That was amazing.' It was all right.

The Children is thought-provoking, but the pace limits some of the character development, leaving me with more unanswered questions than answers, which at times distracts from the bigger message at the heart of this play.
Moving, intelligent and beautifully acted, catch ‘The Children’ while you can.
The writing is funny, nonjudgmental and moving in how it brings radioactive threat into a Suffolk living room.

cn.t: Critics find Kirkwood's post-nuclear drama remains timely and thought-provoking a decade later, praising strong performances from Syal, Fox, and Conlon, though some note the play takes too long to reach its central moral questions about generational responsibility.
